<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|acquisible|53|acreage}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''acquisible''' (a̤-kwiz′i-bl), ''a.''   [< L. ''acquis-itus'', pp. of ''acquirere'', acquire (see ''acquire''), + E. ''-ible''.]   Capable of being acquired. [Rare.]

'''acquisite†''' (ak′wi-zit), ''a.''   [< L. ''acquisitus'', gained, pp. of ''acquirere'', gain: see ''acquire''. Cf. ''exquisite'', ''requisite''.]   Acquired; gained.
{{smaller block|A humour is a liquid or fluent part of the body, comprehended in it, for the preservation of it; and is either innate or born with us, or adventitious and ''acquisite''.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 95.}}}}

'''acquisition''' (ak-wi-zish′o̤n), ''n.''   [< L. ''acquisitio(n-)'', acquisition, < ''acquirere'': see ''acquire''.]   '''1.''' The act of acquiring or gaining possession: as, the ''acquisition'' of property.
{{smaller block|Any European state may be restrained from pursuing plans of ''acquisition'', or making preparations looking toward future acquisitions, which are judged to be hazardous to the independence . . . of its neighbors.
{{right|''Woolsey'', Introd. to Inter. Law, § 43.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is acquired or gained; especially, a material possession obtained by any means, but sometimes used in the plural of mental gains.
{{smaller block|The Cromwellians were induced to relinquish one third of their ''acquisitions''. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., v.}}}}
{{smaller block|They learn so fast and convey the result so fast as to outrun the logic of their slow brother and make his ''acquisitions'' poor. {{right|''Emerson'', Woman.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''Acquirements'', ''Acquisitions'', etc. See ''acquirement''.}}

'''acquisitive''' (a̤-kwiz′i-tiv), ''a.''   [< L. as if *''acquisitivus'', < ''acquisitus'', pp.: see ''acquisite''.]   '''1†.''' Acquired.
{{smaller block|He died not in his ''acquisitive'', but in his native soil.
{{right|''Wotton'', Reliquiæ, p. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|The first condition then of mental development is that the attitude of the mind should be creative rather than ''acquisitive''.
{{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, I. 105.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Acquisitive faculty''', in ''psychol.'', perception; the presentative faculty.}}

'''acquisitively''' (a̤-kwiz′i-tiv-li), ''adv.'' In an acquisitive manner; by way of acquisition.

'''acquisitiveness''' (a̤-kwiz′i-tiv-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The quality of being acquisitive; a propensity to acquire property.—'''2.''' In ''phren.'', the organ to which is attributed the function of producing the general desire to acquire and possess, apart from the uses of the objects. Sometimes called ''covetiveness''. See cut under ''phrenology''.

'''acquist†''' (a-kwist′), ''n.''   [A form of ''acquest'', after It. ''acquisto'', ML. ''acquistum'', L. ''acquisitum''.]   Acquest; acquirement.
{{smaller block|<poem>New ''acquist''
Of true experience.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1755.}}}}

'''acquit''' (a̤-kwit′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''acquitted'', ppr. ''acquitting''.   [< ME. ''aquiten'', ''acwiten'', < OF. ''aquiter'', ''acuiter'', later ''acquiter'', “to quit, acquit, free, clear, discharge, rid of, deliver from” (Cotgrave), F. ''acquitter'' = Pr. ''aquitar'' = It. ''acquetare'', appease, quiet, < ML. *''acquitare'', ''acquietare'', settle a claim, appease, quiet, < L. ''ad'', to, + ''quietare'', quiet, < ''quietus'', discharged, free, at rest, quiet: see ''acquiet'', ''quiet'', and ''quit''.]   '''1.''' To release or discharge, as from an obligation, accusation, guilt, censure, suspicion, or whatever is laid against or upon a person as a charge or duty; specifically, in ''law'', to pronounce not guilty: as, we ''acquit'' a man of evil intentions; the jury ''acquitted'' the prisoner. {{smaller|It is followed by ''of'' before the thing of which one is acquitted; to ''acquit from'' is obsolete.}}
{{smaller block|His poverty, can you ''acquit'' him ''of'' that?
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Duenna, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|If he [Bacon] was convicted, it was because it was impossible to ''acquit'' him without offering the grossest outrage to justice and common sense. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
'''2.''' To atone for. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Till life to death ''acquit'' my forced offence.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1071.}}}}
'''3.''' To settle, as a debt; requite; pay; discharge; fulfil.
{{smaller block|''Aquyte'' hym wel for goddes love, quod he.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1200.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Midst foes (as champion of the faith) he ment
That palme or cypress should his paines ''acquite''.</poem>
{{right|''Carew'', Tasso.}}}}
{{smaller block|I admit it to be not so much the duty as the privilege of an American citizen to ''acquit'' this obligation to the memory of his fathers with discretion and generosity.
{{right|''Everett'', Orations, I. 382.}}}}
{{smaller block|We see young men who owe us a new world, so readily and lavishly they promise, but they never ''acquit'' the debt.
{{right|''Emerson'', Experience.}}}}
'''4.''' With a reflexive pronoun: (''a'') To clear one’s self.
{{smaller block|Pray God he may ''acquit him'' [himself] of suspicion!
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}
(''b'') To behave; bear or conduct one’s self: as, the soldier ''acquitted himself'' well in battle; the orator ''acquitted himself'' indifferently.
{{smaller block|Though this was one of the first mercantile transactions of my life, yet I had no doubt about ''acquitting myself'' with reputation.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xiv.}}}}
'''5†.''' To release; set free; rescue.
{{smaller block|Till I have ''acquit'' your captive Knight.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. vii. 52.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' '''1.''' To exonerate, exculpate, discharge, set free. See ''absolve.''—'''4.''' (''b'') To behave, act, bear, conduct, demean, deport, or quit (one’s self).}}

'''acquit†.''' Past participle of ''acquit.''
{{smaller block|I am glad I am so ''acquit'' of this tinder-box.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 3.}}}}

'''acquite†''' (ạ-kwīt′), ''v. t.'' Same as ''acquit.''   [Compare ''requite.'']

'''acquitment''' (ạ-kwit′mẹnt), ''n.'' The act of acquitting, or the state of being acquitted; acquittal. [Rare.]

'''acquittal''' (ạ-kwit′ạl), ''n.''   [< ME. ''acquitalle'', ''-ayle''; < ''acquit'' + ''-al.'']   '''1.''' The act of acquitting, or the state of being acquitted. {{smaller|Specifically, in ''law'': (''a'') A judicial setting free or deliverance from the charge of an offense by pronouncing a verdict of not guilty. (''b'') In England, freedom from entries and molestations by a superior lord for services issuing out of lands.   ''Cowell.''}}
'''2.''' Performance, as of a duty; discharge of an obligation or a debt.
{{smaller block|I have been long in arrears to you, but I trust you will take this huge letter as an ''acquittal.''
{{right|''Walpole'', Letter to H. Mann.}}}}

'''acquittance''' (ạ-kwit′ạns), ''n.''   [< ME. ''aquitance'', ''-ans'', ''acquitance'', ''-aunce'', < OF. ''aquitance'', < ''aquiter'', discharge: see ''acquit'' and ''-ance.'']   '''1.''' The act of acquitting or discharging from a debt or any other liability; the state of being so discharged.

{{smaller block|Now must your conscience my ''acquittance'' seal.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 7.}}}}

'''2.''' A writing in evidence of a discharge; a receipt in full, which bars a further demand.

<poem>You can produce ''acquittances''
For such a sum.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., ii. 1.}}}}

'''3†.''' The act of clearing one’s self.

{{smaller block|Being suspected and put for their ''acquittance'' to take the sacrament of the altar.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}}}

'''acquittance†''' (ạ-kwit′ạns), ''v. t.'' To acquit.

<poem>Your mere enforcement shall ''acquittance'' me
From all the impure blots and stains thereof.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 7.}}}}

'''acquittance-roll''' (ạ-kwit′ạns-rōl), ''n.'' In the British army, the pay-roll of a company, troop, or battery.

'''Acræa''' (a-krē′ä̤), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. ἀκραῖος, equiv. to ἄκρος, at the top or extremity.]   A genus of nymphalid butterflies, typical of the subfamily ''Acræinæ''. ''A. antias'' is an example.

'''Acræinæ''' (ak-rē-ī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Acræa'' + ''-inæ''.]   A subfamily of butterflies of the family ''Nymphalidæ'', taking name from the leading genus ''Acræa'', and containing mostly African species of small or moderate size, with semitransparent wings, reddish-brown marked with black. There are about 85 species.

'''Acramphibrya''' (ak-ram-fib′ri-ä̤), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < Gr. ἄκρος, at the end, + ἀμφί, on both sides, + βρύον, a flower, blossom, < βρύειν, swell, be full to bursting.]   In ''bot.'', a term used by Endlicher as a class name for exogenous plants, which he described as plants growing both at the apex and at the sides.

'''acrania''' (a-krā′ni-ä̤), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. ἀ- priv. + κρανίον, L. ''cranium'', the skull.]   '''1.''' [NL., fem. sing.] In ''teratol.'', a malformation consisting in an entire absence of the bones and integuments forming the vault of the skull. Also written ''acrany''.—'''2.''' [''cap.''] [NL., neut. pl.] A name proposed by Haeckel as a class designation for ''Amphioxus'' or ''Branchiostoma''; a synonym of ''Myelozoa'' or ''Leptocardia'' (which see). Also called ''Acephala''. See ''Amphioxus'' and ''Branchiostoma''.

'''acranial''' (a-krā′ni-a̤l), ''a.''   [See ''acrania''.]   Having no skull.

'''acrany''' (ak′rā-ni), ''n.'' Same as ''acrania'', 1.

'''acrase†''', ''v. t.'' See ''acraze''.

'''acrasia†''', ''n.'' See ''acrasy''.

'''Acraspeda, Acraspedota''' (a-kras′pe-dä̤, a-kras-pe-dō′tä̤), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < Gr. ἀ- priv. + κράσπεδον, a hem or border.]   The name given by Gegenbaur to the acalephs proper; that is, to those jelly-fishes and sea-nettles the lobate border of whose disk is not provided (with few exceptions, as in ''Aurelia'') with a contractile marginal fold or velum: nearly synonymous with ''Discophora'' (which see): opposed to ''Craspedota''. See cut under ''acaleph''.

'''acraspedote''' (a-kras′pe-dōt), ''a.''   [< Gr. ἀ- priv. (''a''-<sup>18</sup>) + ''craspedote'', or as ''Acraspeda'' + ''-ote''.]   Having no velum, as a discophore; of or pertaining to the ''Acraspeda.''
{{smaller block|The Hydroidea and Siphonophora are craspedote; the Discophora are supposed to be destitute of a veil, and are therefore ''acraspedote.''
{{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', I. 94.}}}}

'''acrasy†''', '''acrasia†''' (ak′ra-si, a-krā′zi-ä̤), ''n.''   [< ML. ''acrasia'', which appears to combine the notions of (1) Gr. ἀκρασία, later form of ἀκράτεια, intemperance, want of self-control (< ἀκρατής, wanting in self-control, intemperate, unbridled, < ἀ- priv. + κράτος, strength, power, akin to E. ''hard'', q. v.); and (2) Gr. ἀκρασία, bad mixture, ill temperature, < ἄκρατος, unmixed, untempered, intemperate, excessive, < ἀ- priv. + *κρατός, mixed: see ''crater'' and ''crasis.'']   Excess; surfeit; intemperance; incontinence.
{{smaller block|''Acrasies'', whether of the body or mind, occasion great uneasiness.
{{right|''Cornish'', Life of Firmin, p. 84.}}}}

'''acratia''' (a-krā′shiä̤), ''n.''   [< Gr. ἀκράτεια, want of power: see ''acrasy.'']   In ''pathol.'', failure of strength; weakness; debility.

'''acraze†''', '''acrase†''' (a-krāz′), ''v. t.''   [< F. ''acraser'', “''accrazer'', break, burst, craze, bruise, crush” (Cotgrave), same as ''écraser'', ''escraser'', “to squash down, beat flat,” etc. (Cotgrave): see ''a-''<sup>11</sup>, ''a-''<sup>15</sup>, and ''craze.'']   To weaken, impair, or enfeeble in mind, body, or estate.
{{smaller block|I ''acrazed'' was.
{{right|''Mir. for Mags.'', p. 138.}}}}
{{smaller block|My substance impaired, my credit ''acrased.''
{{right|''Gascoigne'', Letter in Hermit’s Tale, p. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|Cold in the night which ''acraseth'' the bodie.
{{right|''Holinshed'', Chronicles, III. 1049.}}}}

'''acre''' (ā′kėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''aker'', ''akir'', a field, an acre, < AS. ''æcer'', a field, later also an acre, = OS. ''akkar'' = OFries. ''ekker'' = D. ''akker'' = OHG. ''ahhar'', ''achar'', ''accar'', MHG. G. ''acker'' = Icel. ''akr'' = Sw. ''åker'' = Dan. ''ager'' = Goth. ''akrs'' = L. ''ager'' = Gr. ἀγρός = Skt. ''ajra'', all in the sense of field, orig. a pasture or a chase, hunting-ground; < √ *''ag'', Skt. √ ''aj'' = Gr. ἄγειν = L. ''agere'' = Icel. ''aka'', drive: see ''ake'' = ''ache''<sup>1</sup>, and (< L. ''agere'') ''act'', etc. Hence ''acorn'', q. v. The spelling ''acre'' instead of the reg. ''aker'' (cf. ''baker'', AS. ''bæcere'') is due to its legal use in imitation of OF. ''acre'', < ML. (Law L.) ''acra'', ''acrum'', from Teut.]   '''1.''' Originally, an open plowed or sowed field. {{smaller|This signification was gradually lost after the acre was made a definite measure of surface. Still used in the plural to denote fields or land in general.}}
{{smaller block|My bosky ''acres'', and my unshrubb’d down.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Over whose ''acres'' walked those blessed feet.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' A superficial measure of land, usually stated to be 40 poles in length by 4 in breadth; but 160 perches (= 4840 square yards, or 43,560 square feet) make an acre, however shaped. {{smaller|An acre, as a specific quantity of land, was reckoned in England as much as a yoke of oxen could plow in a day till the establishment of a definite measure by laws of the thirteenth century and later. This is known in Great Britain and the United States as the statute acre, to distinguish it from the customary acres still in use to some extent in Scotland, Ireland, and Wales. The Scotch acre is larger than the statute acre, as it contains 6150.4 square yards, 48 Scotch acres being equal to 61 statute acres. The Irish acre is 7840 square yards, 100 Irish acres being nearly equivalent to 162 statute acres. In Wales different measures, the ''erw'', the ''stang'', the ''paladr'', are called ''acres''. The true erw is 4320 square yards; the stang is 3240. There is also the Cornish acre, of 5760 square yards. Among the customary English acres are found measures of the following numbers of perches: 80 (of hops), 90 (of hops), 107, 110, 120 (shut acre), 130, 132, 134, 141, 180 (forest acre), 200 (for copyhold land in Lincolnshire), 212, 256 (of wood). The Leicestershire acre has 2308⅔ square yards, the Westmoreland acre 6760 square yards, the Cheshire acre 10,240 square yards. Often abbreviated to ''A.'' or ''a.''}}

{{smaller block|The ''acre'' was in many cases a small field simply, ''i. e.'', an ''ager;'' and a hundred and twenty small fields were called a hide. A standard ''acre'' was hardly established until the thirteenth century.
{{right|''D. W. Ross'', German Land-holding, Notes, p. 131.}}}}

'''3†.''' A lineal measure equal to a furrow’s length, or 40 poles; more frequently, an acre’s breadth, 4 poles, equal to 22 or 25 yards.—'''Burgh acres.''' {{smaller|See ''burgh''.}}—'''God’s acre.''' {{smaller|See ''God’s-acre''.}}

'''acreable''' (ā′kėr-a̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''acre'' + ''-able''.]   According to the acre; measured or estimated in acres or by the acre.

{{smaller block|The ''acreable'' produce of the two methods was nearly the same.
{{right|''Complete Farmer'', Art. Potatoe (Ord. MS.).}}}}

'''acreage''' (ā′kėr-ạ̄j), ''n.''   [< ''acre'' + ''-age''.]   The number of acres in a piece or tract of land; acres taken collectively; extent in acres: as, the ''acreage'' of farm-land in a country; the ''acreage'' of wheat sown.

<poem>No coarse and blockish God of ''acreage''
Stands at thy gate for thee to grovel to.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}
{{smaller block|The interests of a nation of our ''acreage'' and population are a serious load to be conducted safely.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLI. 211.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
